production.title: $6.3B crypto heist: Experts explain to the biggest theft in history

narration:
The exchange had already stopped withdrawals,
but one of its wallets could still authorize more transactions.
That is the detail at the centre of the reported $6.3 billion Binance theft.
The attackers did not necessarily steal one master private
key and walk straight into a digital vault.
According to Binance’s own investigation,
they got into the software and permissions surrounding the vault,
then used a trusted signing system to make unauthorized transactions look valid.
In the next few minutes, we’ll follow that attack from one compromised work computer,
through stolen credentials and an internal signing service,
to a permission written onto Ethereum that kept working even after withdrawals were paused.
And we’ll answer the question that sounds simple but isn’t:
if the exchange stopped withdrawals,
why did it still need another blockchain transaction to take control back?
Let’s start with the part that confused a lot of people.
When an exchange says withdrawals are suspended,
you imagine the cash register being switched off.
Customers can no longer request money, so the payments should stop.
That is what happened to the normal withdrawal system.
But the wallet involved in this incident had
also been given another set of instructions, directly on the blockchain.
Those instructions could operate outside the ordinary withdrawal process.
A crypto transaction is not just a message saying,
“please send these coins.” It is a signed instruction that
the blockchain accepts as coming from an authorized wallet.
The important question is not only who owns the wallet,
but which software is allowed to prepare and approve those instructions.
Binance says the attack began on October 29, 2026,
with a compromised employee work computer.
The company’s November 3 initial findings say the attacker then moved through internal systems,
eventually reaching the machinery that handles wallet signing.
So the story is not a stranger guessing a password at the front door.
It is closer to someone getting into an employee’s office,
finding the tools used by the security team,
and then persuading the official door system to approve the wrong person.
But how do you get from one work computer
to a system connected to billions of dollars?
That path is where the attack becomes more complicated.
According to Binance, the compromised computer was only the beginning.
The attacker used access to an internal AI tool
to reach additional people who worked on wallet infrastructure.
From there, the attacker discovered a token with permission to deploy containers.
A container is a packaged piece of software
that can run inside an internal system.
Think of it as a sealed workbench.
It contains the program and the parts that program needs,
but the workbench can still be connected to powerful tools outside it.
The attacker then used stolen credentials to access another engineer’s computer, deployed a container,
and triggered a malicious script.
Binance says that script reached the internal wallet-signing service.
You might be wondering why a signing service
would be able to do this at all.
The answer is that the service has a real job.
It must authorize legitimate transfers across the exchange’s wallets.
If it could only sign one narrow type of customer withdrawal,
it would be less useful, but also easier to design.
The danger appears when the same service can be reached through a different route,
with credentials that were trusted but being used by the wrong person.
The normal withdrawal screen may say no.
The signing service may still receive a request that looks technically valid.
This is also why the phrase “the private key was
not stolen” does not automatically mean the money was safe.
A key is one part of the lock.
The software deciding when to use that key is another part.
Binance says the affected hot wallet used multi-party computation, or MPC.
Instead of keeping one complete private key in one place,
MPC spreads the signing process across multiple parties and systems.
No single person is supposed to hold a
complete key that can immediately empty the wallet.
That is stronger than a single password, but it creates a different security boundary.
If an attacker gains enough access to the trusted
software and permissions around the distributed signing process,
they may be able to cause an authorized signature without extracting one master key.
The missing piece is what that service was authorized to sign.
On Ethereum, the answer included a powerful on-chain delegation.
The signing service was the hand that approved transactions,
but Ethereum had already given that hand a new instruction.
The instruction used EIP-7702, a feature described in the official Ethereum specification.
It allows an ordinary Ethereum account to point to contract code and say,
in effect, “when this account is called,
use these instructions.” Picture the hot wallet as a vault.
Normally, the vault follows its owner’s signed instructions.
With this delegation,
the owner signs a note that tells the
vault to let a robot operate inside it.
The robot is not magic.
It is contract code.
But calls to the account can then run that code in the account’s context,
giving the code access to the account’s assets and capabilities.
Binance says the attackers used the signing system to write this
kind of delegation from the affected hot wallet to attacker-controlled code.
That meant the attackers did not have to
keep asking the normal withdrawal system for permission.
They had created another route for the wallet to act.
This is the point where the attack stops looking like
a stolen password and starts looking like a permissions failure.
The attacker got the official signing machinery to approve a change,
and that change was then recorded on Ethereum.
Why does that matter?
Because blockchains do not forget an instruction simply because
a company shuts down one of its computers.
Once the delegation was written on-chain, it became part of the wallet’s current state.
The attacker’s code could now behave like a robot with a standing order.
The exchange could turn off the normal operator,
but the robot was no longer waiting for that operator’s dashboard.
And that leaves us with the strange moment in this story: Binance paused withdrawals,
yet the malicious authorization still had to be removed separately.
Stopping withdrawals closed the exchange’s ordinary payment route.
It did not erase the permission that had already been written to Ethereum.
That is why the pause was not enough.
The malicious delegation operated independently of the normal withdrawal infrastructure.
If new assets reached the affected wallet,
the attacker’s code could still be positioned to act on them.
You might be wondering why Binance could not simply
change a password or shut down the compromised container.
Those steps could block the attacker from using the internal system again,
but they could not rewrite the blockchain by themselves.
The wallet had to authorize another blockchain transaction.
Under EIP-7702, delegating to the 0 address clears the delegation.
In everyday terms,
the vault had to sign a new note
saying that the robot no longer had control.
Binance says it submitted additional transactions to revoke the malicious authorizations and eventually
executed a new authorization from the affected hot wallet to the 0 address.
Notice the order here.
First, the company had to regain control of the signing process.
Then it had to use that control on-chain.
Only after that could the old delegation be cleared.
This also explains why a distributed wallet system did not make recovery instant.
MPC may prevent one complete private key from sitting on one laptop,
but the organization still needs secure software,
secure credentials and secure approval paths around it.
If those surrounding permissions are abused,
the strongest part of the system may be bypassed in practice.
The unanswered question is how much access the
attacker had before the delegation was created,
and whether every affected system has now been identified.
So what does this incident actually prove?
First, it shows that crypto security is not only about protecting private keys.
It is also about protecting the computers, deployment tokens,
credentials and signing services that are allowed to use those keys.
Second,
“no master key was stolen” is not the same as “the wallet could not
be moved.” Binance’s report describes an attack on the process around the key:
a work computer, internal access, a container-deployment permission,
stolen credentials and a signing service that could authorize transactions outside the usual path.
Third, a blockchain permission can outlive the system that created it.
The exchange could pause withdrawals in seconds,
but the delegation remained until another valid blockchain authorization removed it.
And there is an honest limitation here.
Binance’s initial findings explain the reported route and the response,
but they do not answer every question about how the first computer was compromised,
how the credentials were obtained, or why the signing service accepted the unauthorized request.
Those details matter because the same failure could happen again if the
organization fixes only the visible container and not the permissions around it.
The real lesson is simple: the vault was not protected by one lock.
It was protected by a chain of software and people,
and the attackers found a way to make that chain approve them.
At the beginning, withdrawals had stopped,
but the wallet was still able to act because
a permission had already been written onto the blockchain.
The attackers may not have needed one master key.
They needed access to the hands that could make the wallet sign,
and then they used Ethereum’s own rules to
leave a robot standing inside the vault.
Binance eventually had to sign its way back
out by delegating to the 0 address.
That is why this was not just a stolen-key story.
It was a compromised computer becoming trusted software, trusted software reaching a signing service,
and a valid permission becoming the hardest part to undo.
Follow the channel for the next update,
because the full post-mortem should tell us whether the real failure
was finally closed or only the first route into the vault.

research.summary: The incident illustrates a permissions-and-signing failure rather than a simple “the hackers stole the master private key” failure. Binance says attackers first compromised an employee’s work computer, used an internal AI tool to reach other wallet-infrastructure personnel, discovered a container-deployment token, and later used stolen credentials to access another engineer’s computer, deploy a container, and trigger a malicious script. That script reached the internal wallet-signing service, which could authorize transactions outside Binance’s ordinary withdrawal workflow. On Ethereum, the attackers used EIP-7702 to write an on-chain delegation from a hot wallet to attacker-controlled contract code. Because Binance’s wallet used multi-party computation, there was no single private key to extract or immediately use; the attackers instead abused trusted software, credentials, and signing permissions. Suspending withdrawals stopped the normal withdrawal pipeline, but it did not erase the delegation already recorded on-chain. Binance therefore had to submit additional blockchain transactions to revoke the authorization, ultimately clearing the delegation by authorizing the zero address.

claims.claim: Binance’s reported attack path began with a compromised work computer. The attacker used an internal AI tool to reach additional wallet-infrastructure employees, found a container-deployment permission token, then used stolen credentials to access another engineer’s computer, deploy a container, and trigger a malicious script.

claims.claim: The attackers obtained unauthorized access to an internal wallet-signing service and used it to initiate transactions outside Binance’s normal withdrawal process.
claims.source_title: 29 October 2026 Binance Security Incident: Initial Findings and Response Update

claims.claim: The key security boundary was the signing service and its permissions: access to the service allowed the attacker to cause valid-looking blockchain authorizations and transactions, even though the public report does not say that a single master private key was stolen.
claims.source_title: 29 October 2026 Binance Security Incident: Initial Findings and Response Update

claims.claim: Binance says the affected hot wallet used multi-party computation, meaning there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious authorization. This supports describing the incident as abuse of a distributed signing process and its surrounding permissions, rather than assuming extraction of one master key.
claims.source_title: 29 October 2026 Binance Security Incident: Initial Findings and Response Update

claims.claim: EIP-7702 allows an externally owned account to set a delegation pointer to contract code. Calls to the account can then execute the delegated code in the account’s context, allowing the account’s assets and capabilities to be controlled through that code.

The delegation is persistent on-chain until changed. EIP-7702 specifies that delegating to the zero address clears the delegation, which is why revocation requires a new blockchain authorization rather than merely shutting down an internal service.

Stopping withdrawals was not sufficient because the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations already existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure. Binance says it had to submit additional transactions to revoke them.
claims.source_title: 29 October 2026 Binance Security Incident: Initial Findings and Response Update

claims.claim: Binance reports that it eventually executed a new authorization from the affected hot wallet to the zero address, clearing the EIP-7702 delegation.

metadata.title: $6.3B crypto heist: Experts explain to the biggest theft in history
metadata.description:
This video explains the reported $6.3 billion Binance theft and how attackers moved from a compromised employee computer to stolen credentials, an internal wallet-signing service, and an Ethereum hot wallet delegation. The attack reportedly used trusted software and permissions rather than stealing one complete master private key.

You’ll see why pausing withdrawals was not enough, how EIP-7702 gave attacker-controlled code a route into the wallet, and why Binance needed to authorize another blockchain transaction to clear the malicious delegation. The incident shows how crypto security depends on the entire chain of computers, credentials, software, and signing systems around a private key.

0:00 Intro
0:51 The Stopped Withdrawals
2:13 The Compromised Computer
4:21 The Signing Service
6:05 The Blockchain Robot
7:48 Why Stopping Failed
9:13 Intro
